narrative: The model estimated a 58% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure to be somewhat more likely than passing, and the law school treated that risk as too high, so your application was denied. The strongest factor by far was your third-year class standing: you were in the second decile, well below the average of about the sixth decile among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA were the next most influential factors. Although both were below the averages for accepted students—34 versus about 37, and 2.60 versus about 3.23—in this particular prediction they acted as relative strengths, reducing the predicted risk of failure rather than increasing it. They were not enough to offset the concern raised by your third-year academic standing. To move forward, ask the admissions office whether additional context or supporting documents can be considered. Focus on strengthening the area that drove the decision: seek advising about your third-year coursework and whether further academic work, a clearer explanation of your record, or a revised application can demonstrate readiness. You may also consider retaking the LSAT or improving your GPA through additional study, and applying to programs that review applicants holistically.
